questions.question: What is Google Spanner's TrueTime API and what hardware does it rely on?
options: A software-only clock synchronization protocol similar to NTP
An API backed by GPS receivers and atomic clocks that returns a time interval with guaranteed bounds
A distributed timestamp service that uses Raft consensus
A logical clock implementation based on Lamport timestamps
questions.explanation: TrueTime uses GPS receivers and atomic clocks in every Google datacenter to provide a time interval [earliest, latest] that is guaranteed to contain the true current time. This bounded uncertainty enables Spanner to assign globally meaningful timestamps to transactions.

questions.question: How does CockroachDB replicate data for fault tolerance?
options: Master-slave replication with asynchronous followers
Raft consensus per range, with each range replicated across multiple nodes
Two-phase commit across all nodes for every write
Gossip protocol for eventual consistency
questions.explanation: CockroachDB splits data into ranges (default 512MB) and replicates each range using Raft consensus. Each range has a Raft leader that serializes writes and replicates them to followers. If the leader fails, Raft elects a new leader within seconds.

questions.question: What partitioning strategy does DynamoDB use to distribute data across nodes?
options: Range-based partitioning sorted by primary key
Consistent hashing to map partition keys to storage nodes
Round-robin distribution across all available nodes
Manual sharding configured by the application developer
questions.explanation: DynamoDB uses consistent hashing to map each partition key to a position on a hash ring, then assigns it to the responsible node. This ensures even distribution and minimal data movement when nodes are added or removed.

questions.question: What does 'external consistency' mean in the context of Google Spanner?
options: Data is consistent with external systems like message queues
If transaction A commits before transaction B starts, A's commit timestamp is guaranteed to be less than B's
Data is encrypted when sent to external clients
External users always see the latest committed data
questions.explanation: External consistency (also called strict serializability) means the transaction order matches real-time order. If any observer sees A complete before B starts, then A's timestamp is less than B's in the database. Spanner achieves this using TrueTime's commit-wait protocol.

questions.question: What is a sloppy quorum in DynamoDB, and how does it differ from a strict quorum?
options: A quorum that allows any W nodes to acknowledge a write, even if they are not the designated replicas for that key
A quorum that requires all replicas to acknowledge before returning success
A quorum that uses random nodes for each operation
A quorum that only works during network partitions
questions.explanation: In a strict quorum, writes and reads must go to the designated replica nodes. A sloppy quorum allows writes to be accepted by any W available nodes, even non-designated ones (hinted handoff). This improves availability during failures but can temporarily violate consistency.

questions.question: Why does CockroachDB use hybrid-logical clocks (HLC) instead of TrueTime?
options: HLC is faster than TrueTime
CockroachDB runs on commodity hardware without GPS/atomic clock infrastructure, and HLC combines physical and logical timestamps to provide causal ordering
HLC provides stronger consistency guarantees than TrueTime
TrueTime is patented and cannot be used outside Google
questions.explanation: HLC combines a physical timestamp (from NTP-synchronized clocks) with a logical counter to ensure causal ordering even when physical clocks drift. Unlike TrueTime, it doesn't need specialized hardware, making it suitable for commodity deployments.

questions.question: In Spanner's commit-wait protocol, why does the transaction coordinator wait for TrueTime's uncertainty interval to pass before reporting commit success?
options: To allow replicas time to apply the write
To ensure no future transaction can receive a timestamp earlier than this transaction's commit timestamp, guaranteeing external consistency
To reduce network congestion between datacenters
To give clients time to process the previous response
questions.explanation: The commit-wait ensures that the assigned timestamp is definitely in the past by the time the commit is reported. This means any subsequent transaction will get a later timestamp, preserving real-time ordering. The wait is typically 7ms (the TrueTime uncertainty bound).

questions.question: DynamoDB originally used vector clocks to detect conflicting writes. What problem do vector clocks solve, and why did DynamoDB eventually move away from them?
options: Vector clocks measure latency; they were replaced by faster timers
Vector clocks track causal history to detect conflicts, but they grow in size with the number of writers, creating metadata bloat and requiring application-level conflict resolution
Vector clocks encrypt timestamps; they were replaced by TLS
Vector clocks synchronize physical clocks; they were replaced by NTP
questions.explanation: Vector clocks attach a version vector to each item, tracking which nodes wrote which versions. This detects concurrent conflicting writes. However, the vectors grow with the number of distinct writers, adding storage overhead. DynamoDB later moved to last-writer-wins with server-side timestamps for simplicity.

questions.question: CockroachDB range splits occur when a range exceeds 512MB. What happens to the Raft group when a range splits?
options: The Raft group is dissolved and a new one is formed
The range splits into two new ranges, each getting its own independent Raft group with its own leader election
The Raft group stays the same but handles two ranges
Range splits are handled by a central coordinator, not Raft
questions.explanation: When a range splits, the original Raft group is split into two independent Raft groups. Each new range gets its own leader, its own replication, and its own log. The split is itself a replicated operation recorded in the Raft log to ensure all replicas split consistently.

questions.question: You need a globally distributed database for a financial application requiring strict transaction ordering. Which database and why?
options: DynamoDB — its single-digit millisecond latency ensures fast transactions
Google Spanner — TrueTime provides external consistency guaranteeing real-time transaction ordering across the globe
CockroachDB — Raft consensus is the strongest consistency model available
Any database with read replicas would work equally well
questions.explanation: Financial applications requiring strict global ordering need external consistency — if transaction A completes before B starts anywhere in the world, A must appear first in the database. Only Spanner (via TrueTime) provides this guarantee at global scale without cross-region coordination delays.
